section.title: Introduction to Queues
section.content: A queue is a fundamental linear data structure that strictly follows the FIFO principle: First In First Out. This means that the first element inserted into the queue will be the first one to be removed, preserving the natural order of arrival. Queues are widely used in computer science to model real-world scenarios where order and fairness matter, such as a line of customers waiting at a bank counter, a printer job queue, or a CPU task scheduler. Unlike a stack, which operates on a LIFO (Last In First Out) basis, a queue ensures that no element is processed out of turn. The two ends of a queue have specific roles: the rear (also called the tail or back) is where new elements are added, and the front (also called the head) is where elements are removed.

bulletPoints.point: 📌 FIFO: First In First Out — the fundamental principle governing queue behavior
▶️ Insertion at the rear (enqueue) — new elements always join at the back
▶️ Removal at the front (dequeue) — elements leave from the front of the queue
▶️ Two distinct ends: front (exit point) and rear (entry point)
▶️ Preserves the chronological order of element insertion
📊 Contrast with Stack (LIFO) and Priority Queue (ordered by priority)
▶️ Real-world analogies: supermarket checkout line, airport boarding queue, ticket counter
🎯 Applications: OS scheduling, network packet handling, BFS graph traversal

section.title: Operations on Queues
section.content: A queue supports a well-defined set of operations that allow efficient management of its elements. Each operation has a specific role and, when implemented correctly, runs in constant time O(1). The core operations are Enqueue and Dequeue, but auxiliary operations such as Peek, IsEmpty, IsFull, and Size are equally important for building robust programs. Understanding both the behavior and the time complexity of each operation is essential for choosing the right implementation in a given context. Improper use — such as attempting to dequeue from an empty queue — leads to underflow errors and must be guarded against with proper checks.

bulletPoints.point: 🔧 Enqueue (push/offer): insert a new element at the rear of the queue — O(1)
🔧 Dequeue (pop/poll): remove and return the element at the front of the queue — O(1)
🔧 Peek / Front: inspect the front element without removing it — O(1)
⚡ Rear / Back: inspect the last inserted element without removing it — O(1)
🔧 IsEmpty: returns true if the queue contains no elements — O(1)
🔧 IsFull: returns true if the queue has reached its maximum capacity (array-based) — O(1)
🔧 Size / Count: returns the current number of elements in the queue — O(1)
🔧 Clear / Flush: removes all elements from the queue at once
⚠️ Overflow error: attempting to enqueue into a full queue (fixed-size implementations)
⚠️ Underflow error: attempting to dequeue from an empty queue — must always be checked

section.title: Implementation with an Array
section.content: One of the simplest ways to implement a queue is by using a static array combined with two integer indices: front and rear. The front index always points to the first valid element, while the rear index points to the position of the last inserted element. Enqueue increments rear and stores the new value; Dequeue reads the value at front and then increments front. Although this approach is easy to understand and implement, it has a significant drawback: as elements are dequeued, the front pointer advances, leaving unused memory slots at the beginning of the array that can never be reused. This leads to a phenomenon called data displacement, which wastes memory and eventually makes the array appear full even when it still has free space at the start. This limitation motivates the use of a circular queue instead.

bulletPoints.point: ▶️ Uses a fixed-size array T[0..maxSize-1] as the underlying storage
▶️ front index: initialized to 0, points to the oldest element in the queue
▶️ rear index: initialized to -1 (or 0 depending on convention), points to the latest element
⚠️ Enqueue operation: rear++ then T[rear] = value (check for overflow first)
⚠️ Dequeue operation: value = T[front] then front++ (check for underflow first)
▶️ IsEmpty condition: front > rear
▶️ IsFull condition: rear == maxSize - 1
▶️ Size: rear - front + 1
⚡ Time complexity: O(1) for all operations
🐢 Space complexity: O(n) where n is the maximum capacity
❌ Critical flaw: memory waste — freed slots at the front cannot be reused
❌ Workaround (costly): shift all elements left after each dequeue — O(n) time
▶️ Better solution: use a circular array to avoid displacement entirely

section.title: Circular Queue
section.content: The circular queue (also called a ring buffer) is an optimized array-based implementation that eliminates the memory waste problem of the simple array queue. Instead of treating the array as a linear sequence, the circular queue treats it as a closed ring: when either index reaches the end of the array, it wraps around to index 0 using the modulo operator. This allows freed slots at the front to be reused as soon as they become available. Managing a circular queue requires careful handling of the full and empty conditions, because both states can result in front == rear depending on the convention used. A common strategy is to intentionally leave one slot unused, so that a full queue satisfies (rear + 1) % size == front, clearly distinguishing it from the empty condition front == rear. Circular queues are widely used in operating systems for I/O buffers and in hardware communication interfaces.

bulletPoints.point: ▶️ Treats the array as a ring: indices wrap around using the modulo operator
🔧 Enqueue: rear = (rear + 1) % size, then T[rear] = value
🔧 Dequeue: value = T[front], then front = (front + 1) % size
▶️ Empty condition: front == rear (the queue holds no valid elements)
▶️ Full condition: (rear + 1) % size == front (one slot is intentionally left empty)
▶️ Maximum usable capacity: size - 1 elements (due to the sentinel slot)
✅ Completely eliminates memory waste caused by index displacement
⚡ All four primary operations remain O(1)
✅ Space efficiency: 100% reuse of available memory slots
▶️ Requires careful boundary checks to avoid overwriting unread data
🎯 Practical uses: kernel I/O ring buffers, audio/video streaming buffers, hardware FIFOs
▶️ Alternative: use a size counter to distinguish full from empty without wasting a slot

section.title: Queue with Linked List
section.content: A queue can also be implemented using a singly linked list, where each node holds a data value and a pointer to the next node. This approach eliminates the fixed-size constraint of array-based implementations: the queue can grow or shrink dynamically as elements are enqueued or dequeued, bounded only by the available heap memory. Two pointers are maintained: head (or front) pointing to the first node to be dequeued, and tail (or rear) pointing to the last node added. Enqueue creates a new node and appends it after the current tail, then advances the tail pointer. Dequeue reads the value at head and moves the head pointer to the next node, freeing the old node. Both operations run in O(1) time. The tradeoff compared to arrays is a higher memory overhead per element due to the pointer stored in each node, and reduced cache locality since nodes are scattered in heap memory.

bulletPoints.point: 🔗 Built on a singly linked list: each node contains data and a next pointer
🔗 head pointer: always points to the front node (next to be dequeued)
🔗 tail pointer: always points to the rear node (last inserted)
🔧 Enqueue: create new node, set tail.next = newNode, then tail = newNode — O(1)
🔧 Dequeue: save head.data, advance head = head.next, free old node — O(1)
▶️ IsEmpty condition: head == null (or head == tail in some implementations)
✅ Dynamic sizing: no predefined capacity limit — grows with heap availability
✅ No overflow risk (unless the system runs out of memory)
✅ No memory waste: each node is allocated and freed on demand
❌ Tradeoff: extra memory per node (the next pointer, typically 8 bytes on 64-bit systems)
❌ Tradeoff: poor cache locality — nodes are scattered across heap memory
▶️ Suitable when queue size is unpredictable or varies greatly at runtime
▶️ Thread-safe variants exist (e.g., lock-free linked queues using CAS operations)

section.title: Applications of Queues
section.content: Queues are one of the most practically important data structures in computer science, appearing in a wide range of system-level, algorithmic, and application-level contexts. Their FIFO ordering makes them ideal whenever tasks, requests, or data must be processed in the exact order they arrive, ensuring fairness and predictability. In operating systems, queues underpin process and thread scheduling, where the CPU selects the next task from a ready queue. In networking, queues manage incoming and outgoing packets at routers and switches, and HTTP request queues balance load across web servers. In graph theory, breadth-first search (BFS) relies on a queue to explore nodes level by level, guaranteeing the shortest path in unweighted graphs. Real-time systems use ring-buffer queues for audio and video streaming to absorb timing jitter. Even everyday software features like undo history, print spoolers, and message brokers (Kafka, RabbitMQ) are fundamentally queue-based.

bulletPoints.point: 🎯 CPU process scheduling: the OS ready queue manages threads awaiting CPU time (Round-Robin)
🎯 I/O request queuing: disk and network I/O requests are buffered in kernel queues
🎯 Network packet routing: routers enqueue packets at each hop to manage congestion
🎯 Load balancing: web servers distribute incoming HTTP requests via request queues
🧠 Breadth-First Search (BFS): graph traversal that explores nodes level by level using a queue
🧠 Shortest path in unweighted graphs: BFS with a queue guarantees minimum hop count
🎯 Print spooler: documents are queued and printed in submission order
🎯 Message brokers: Kafka, RabbitMQ, and ActiveMQ implement persistent distributed queues
🎯 Real-time audio/video streaming: ring buffer queues absorb timing jitter between producer and consumer
▶️ Simulation of discrete-event systems: events are processed in chronological order from a queue
🎯 Keyboard and mouse input buffering: hardware events are enqueued before the OS processes them
▶️ Multithreaded producer-consumer pattern: a shared queue decouples data production from consumption
🎯 Call center systems: incoming calls are queued and routed to available agents in order
